passage: The bus to the district hospital only ran twice a day, so Dhruv's father went alone most mornings. Dhruv's little sister Bindu was in a bed there with a bad chest. At home under the tamarind tree, Dhruv spread out his chalk stubs and drew a cow with a crooked smile, a kite and a tiny house with a yellow door for her. His friend Manoj called from the lane, "Come, we are playing kabaddi!" Dhruv hesitated, then ran off and laughed so hard he forgot the hospital for a while. When he came home he tucked the drawings into his father's bag and did not feel bad about the game.

qa.q: How many times a day did the bus to the district hospital run?
qa.a: It only ran twice a day.

qa.q: What might Dhruv have felt when he hesitated before joining the kabaddi game?
qa.a: He was probably torn between sadness for Bindu and the wish to play, perhaps wondering if it was wrong to have fun.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do that helped him stay connected to his sister while she was away?
qa.a: He drew pictures for her, like the cow, the kite and the house, and sent them with his father, so she would know he was thinking of her.

qa.q: How might Bindu feel when she sees the drawings in the hospital?
qa.a: Bindu may feel cheered and less lonely, knowing her brother was thinking of her. 😊

grounding: A child draws pictures for his younger sister in hospital and also plays; he may be sad and happy without guilt.

passage: Ritu had been in the district hospital in Sitapur for five days with typhoid. Every evening, when the bus brought Amma home, Aparna handed her a new drawing for Ritu: the goats, the neem tree, their cat asleep on the grain sack. 'She stuck the cat on the wall by her bed,' Amma reported. On Saturday, the neighbours' children called Aparna to play gilli-danda in the lane. She hesitated at the door. How could she laugh while her little sister lay in a hospital bed? Dadi, shelling peas on the step, looked up. 'Go. Being sad all day won't make her well faster. Play, and then draw her the game.' Aparna played till dusk. That night she drew the gilli flying over the lane, with Ritu cheering from the side.

qa.q: What did Ritu stick on the wall by her bed?
Why did Aparna hesitate at the door?
qa.a: She felt guilty about laughing and playing while her little sister lay in a hospital bed.

qa.q: What did Dadi help Aparna see?
qa.a: That being sad all day won't help Ritu; she can play and still show care by drawing the game for her.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel getting Aparna's drawings?
qa.a: Cheered and connected to home; she even stuck the cat drawing on the wall 😊

grounding: A village girl draws pictures for her sister in hospital and learns she may play without guilt.

passage: Emil's little sister Hana had been in the children's hospital in Copenhagen for two weeks. Every afternoon Emil sat at the kitchen table with his felt-tip pens and drew her something: a whale, a rocket, their dog in a raincoat. Mum took the pictures in when she visited. On Friday his friend invited him to a birthday party at the swimming pool. Emil said no. 'It feels wrong to have fun,' he told Dad. Dad sat down. 'Hana asked me yesterday if you were still going to parties. She wants to hear about them. It's okay to be sad and to have fun in the same week.' Emil went. Afterwards he drew Hana a picture of himself on the big slide, with a speech bubble: 'Next time, you too.'

qa.q: What did Emil draw for Hana after the party?
qa.a: A picture of himself on the big slide, with a speech bubble.

qa.q: Why did Emil first say no to the party?
qa.a: He felt guilty about having fun while Hana was in hospital.

qa.q: What did Dad help Emil understand?
qa.a: That it's okay to be sad and to have fun in the same week, and that Hana wants to hear about his fun.

qa.q: What might Hana want from her brother while she is in hospital?
qa.a: To hear about his life and still feel part of it, which is why she asked about parties.

grounding: A boy whose little sister is in hospital draws for her and learns that having fun is not a betrayal.
